title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6783 – Reuters estimate
body: Earlier this week: China's PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD - The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

title: Philippines Inflation Rate Surges to 7.8%
body: The annual inflation rate in the Philippines rose to 7.8% in October 2026 from 7.2% in September, surpassing market expectations of 7.6% and reaching its highest level since February 2023. Transport inflation jumped to 20.1% from 14.6%, while inflation for housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels climbed to 9.3% from 8.4%. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy costs in the Philippines, which is highly dependent on supplies from the region. Price pressures also intensified in several other categories: restaurants and accommodation services (7.7% vs 7%), health (5.9% vs 5.6%), and furnishings and household equipment (5% vs 4.7%). By contrast, inflation for food and non-alcoholic beverages eased to 6.1% from 6.7%. On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased by 0.7% in October, following a 1.0% rise in September. Core inflation accelerated to 5.4%—its highest level since September 2023—from a revised 4.8% in September, also coming in above market expectations of 4.8%. title: The market is telling the hyperscalers it's happy about a slower data center buildout
body: Perhaps the clearest takeaway from Tuesday's US midterms is that data centers are unpopular. After a short-lived construction boom, they provide little ongoing employment and drive up local energy costs. There were 41 local votes on data center curbs and 40 of them are on track to win, with margins in the 75/25% range. Microsoft and Amazon are heavily into the data center business, including huge plans to build more so they should be losers today, right? Wrong. Shares of those two are up around 7% and the market cheers a slower, smaller data center buildout. The market has been hating the massive spending on highly-inflated chips and data center supply chains. In effect, the market is saying that the government is doing for you what you should be doing. Now the companies themselves have been trying to sell Wall Street on data center economics but the cash demands are simply too high and the market has said that the risk-reward isn't convincing. At this point, there might be some reflexivity in company management. Now that they've seen how the stock reacts to data center curbs, they might slow their own ambitions to levels closer to matching free cash flow. If so, that could be a powerful tailwind for the stocks, which have struggled this year. Amazon is particularly compelling as its core business of goods delivery isn't under threat from AI in the same way as a software company like Microsoft.

title: US Q3 productivity +3.6% vs +2.8% expected
body: Prior was +1.4% Unit labor costs -0.7% vs +0.6% expected Prior unit labor costs +1.2% On the face of it, these look strong disinflationary but these numbers are largely ignored by policymakers because they're notoriously volatile and hard to measure. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes its Productivity and Costs report quarterly. A preliminary estimate comes out roughly five weeks after the quarter ends, followed by a revised estimate about a month later that incorporates updated GDP and labor data. The headline measure is labor productivity in the nonfarm business sector, defined as output per hour worked. It's reported as an annualized quarterly rate and as a year-over-year change. Output is derived from GDP, excluding government, households, nonprofits and farms, while hours come from the BLS employment surveys. Productivity growth is the main long-run driver of living standards, because it determines how fast incomes can rise without generating inflation. Unit labor costs measure what businesses pay in compensation to produce one unit of output. They're calculated as hourly compensation divided by productivity. When wages rise faster than productivity, unit labor costs climb, which can squeeze profit margins or push companies to raise prices. That makes the measure a closely watched input in the inflation outlook and in the Federal Reserve's assessment of whether wage growth is consistent with its 2% target.

title: BoE Governor Bailey says there is a case for another 25bps hike if war doesn't end
body: Governor Bailey warned that another 25 bps rate increase could be justified if the conflict in Iran does not come to an end. Bailey stressed that the UK needs to limit the inflationary impact of the conflict, particularly given that domestic inflation pressures were already elevated before the energy shock. However, he pushed back against suggestions that the BoE has acted too late, arguing that the latest decline in oil prices was encouraging but that policymakers cannot place too much weight on short-term developments without clear evidence of a genuine peace process. He also refused to commit to a "two and done" outlook for interest rates, highlighting the uncertainty surrounding the conflict and noting that he hopes to have greater clarity on its outcome by December. Bailey also addressed market pricing, noting that the upward shift in the interest rate curve partly reflects higher risk premia rather than expectations of further policy tightening, describing the current pricing as a reasonable reflection of energy-related risks. On the domestic economy, he pointed to stronger-than-expected business investment. On the inflation outlook, Deputy Governor Dave Ramsden said the downward trend in services price inflation appeared to have slowed or stopped. Lombardelli, meanwhile, noted that consumer-facing businesses were reporting less pricing power than business-to-business companies.

title: What Could Stop the Fed Raising Rates in December?
body: A December rate increase remains the market's expected outcome. Investing.com's rate monitor put the probability of a quarter-percentage-point increase at about 80% on 4 November. Another hold would depart from that expectation, making the evidence that might persuade the Federal Reserve to wait particularly relevant for traders. The Fed raised its benchmark rate to 3.75–4% in September and left it unchanged on 28 October. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan supported the hold, then argued two days later for at least two more quarter-point increases. Her position illustrates how officials can favour further tightening while allowing more time between decisions. A similar pause came in June 2023, when the Fed held rates to assess incoming information and earlier tightening before raising them again in July. This time, the case for waiting depends on whether inflation continues to ease and subdued hiring develops into broader employment weakness. Inflation Has Eased Unevenly The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.6% between September 2025 and September 2026, above the Fed's 2% annual inflation target. Prices excluding food and energy, known as core inflation, increased 0.3% in both August and September 2026. Across the third quarter of 2026, however, core inflation slowed to an annualised 2.5%, from 3.3% in the second quarter. These figures express each quarter's price increases as an annual rate.

His post on X reinforced market expectations that the Trump administration could seek an off-ramp from the conflict rather than escalate the war. Keep in mind, though, that Trump can legally continue military operations against Iran even if Democrats control both the House and the Senate. A diplomatic breakthrough would likely support Solana through improving growth expectations and stronger risk appetite, especially given its higher-beta characteristics. An escalation, on the other hand, could trigger another selloff as growth concerns intensify and investors rotate towards safe-haven assets. title: 2026-11-05 - Martin Schlegel: Transmission and conduct of monetary policy in Switzerland
body: To achieve its mandate, a central bank needs to understand how its actions affect the financial system and the economy. Switzerland is a small open economy with a stable political and institutional environment. This creates a special setting for monetary policy. Our main tool is the SNB policy rate. If necessary, the SNB also uses other measures. Understanding the transmission of our monetary policy to the Swiss economy is important for the SNB in achieving its mandate. Changes in the policy rate affect monetary and financial conditions. Short- and long-term rates change, and asset prices and the exchange rate move. This affects consumption and investment, as well as imports and exports. According to our estimates for Switzerland, both the 10-year interest rate and the exchange rate go up after a policy rate increase. One year after the increase, both inflation and output are lower. How have we applied our monetary policy strategy? In the years after the global financial crisis, policy rates reached very low levels, both in Switzerland and abroad. Safe-haven flows posed a threat to price stability. In such an environment, it was important to supplement interest rate policy with foreign exchange interventions to safeguard price stability. In 2021, after years of low inflation, inflation started to rise globally. Around the world, supply was constrained, demand was strong and monetary policy was loose.

title: WTI crude oil settles at $90.52, up 2.72% as buyers defend key support
body: U.S. crude oil futures settled at $90.52 a barrel on Thursday, up $2.40 or 2.72% from Wednesday's $88.12 settlement. The rebound follows a drop of more than 8% on Wednesday, when the U.S. midterm results raised hopes that a Democratic-controlled Congress would increase pressure on the Trump administration to end the war with Iran. Gulf shipping risk is back in focus On Wednesday, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats would seek to end the war, pointing to Congress's control over spending. By Thursday, traders were again weighing the risk to oil shipments. Reuters reported that at least five vessels had reported incidents in the Gulf since Sunday, citing UK Maritime Trade Operations. Iran's foreign minister also spoke with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts about diplomatic efforts. The prospect of de-escalation helped take some risk premium out of oil on Wednesday. The shipping reports gave traders a reason to put some of it back in on Thursday. Wednesday's U.S. inventory report also showed draws in crude, gasoline and distillates for the week ended October 30. The draws offered some support heading into Thursday's session. Buyers defended $86.65–$86.93. Can they get above $91.56? On the WTI chart, the selloff reached $86.65, right near the 200-day moving average at the time. The 100-day moving average was between that low and the 50% midpoint of the rally from the July low at $86.93. That gave buyers a well-defined area to lean against, and they did.

title: The market is waiting for signals from Donald Trump
body: I spoke to Reuters earlier today about the state of markets and my comments boiled down to this: "There are two ​paths Trump can go down - he can double down on unpopular trade ​wars or he can listen to the electorate and change course," said Adam Button, chief currency analyst at investingLive. That's the crossroads we are at right now and I think it shows some of the tension in markets. An early sign we got was on replacing Pete Hegseth: "No, I think he's doing a very good job." Of course, Trump has said that many times before replacing staff, so I wouldn't take it as the final word. It's worth noting though that George H. W. Bush fired Donald Rumsfeld the day after the 2006 midterms, in large part due to the unpopular Iran war. Trump did also tease at Hegseth taking the Tennessee Senate seat after its senator won the Governorship, soemthing he could in January. Alternatively, House member Thomas Massie has pledge to start impeach Hegseth, and there's ample evidence that they could get the votes to do it, either before or after the new Congress is sworn in. Many Senators will be looking to reframe their anti-war, America First chops and Hegseth is a convenient scapegoat. At the same time, there is a big distinction in how he's removed. If it's from Trump, it will be a sign that he's sick of the Iran war and will end it. If it's Congress, that still leaves a pro-war President in power.

title: Oil cracks are beginning to fall and refineries are pointing to more normalization
body: The price of oil at $89 isn't that big of a problem for consumers or businesses. Crude has come down dramatically this week and a big part of that is expectations that Trump or Congress will find a way to open Hormuz and end the Iran war. That remains to be seen but what hasn't changed is ultra-wide crack spreads. Normalized gasoline would be selling around $3.60-3.75 right now with diesel slightly higher with cracks around $22 (gasoline) and $30 (diesel). Because of all the refining tightness, gasoline has about a 60-cent premium and diesel at about +$2.25. That's proven to be a big problem electorally and won't get better so long as the wars in Ukraine and Iran continue. If anything, they will worsen in time on potentially escalated strikes from Ukraine, Iran, the USA and Houthis. From the looks of it, the prognosis is bad and winter sees higher distillate demand as well for heating. There is a positive sign though, the share prices of refineries are rolling over. Valero is a pure play and it's down 22% since October 13. More broadly, the CRAK refiners ETF is down 16% from the October peak. In mid-October, the product tightness was extreme with $100 cracks. That's narrowed to $77 in jet fuel and even more in distillates. Diesel cracks are at $83 coimpared to $102 in mid-October and $92 on October 23. Notably, cracks haven't come in further in the past few days but refiners continue to fall. That could be a forward-looking indicator or market beta but it's worth watching.
